title: Ramakrishna's snake
hookLine: a snake lying coiled and a snake on the move: is it one snake or two?
carry: shakti is the one reality in motion

cards: A snake lies coiled on a warm rock, perfectly still. Then, without warning, it uncoils and glides off into the grass. Is the still snake one thing and the moving snake another?
Obviously not. It's the same snake, resting, then acting.
Ramakrishna, the Kali priest this path met last week, is remembered using that plain picture to answer an old question, the question at the heart of today: what is Shakti?

teach.h: SHAKTI: POWER, THE ABILITY TO ACT.
teach.b: Shakti is Sanskrit for power, energy, the ability to act.

teach.h: NOT A POWER OWNED, BUT THE ONE.
teach.b: In the stories, a god has a shakti, a power often pictured as a goddess at his side. But in the Shakta traditions, which hold the Goddess as the highest reality, that picture turns over.
Shakti isn't a power that someone else owns. She is the one. The path watched this in the Devi Mahatmya, when she drew every goddess on the battlefield back into herself.
Now the old question. Hindu philosophy also speaks of Brahman, the absolute, beyond change and action. Is the still absolute one thing and the active Goddess another?
The stories told by Ramakrishna's followers say he answered with pictures.

teach.h: FIRE AND ITS POWER TO BURN.
teach.b: Fire and its power to burn: you can't have one without the other. Milk and its whiteness. A gem and its shine.
And the snake. When the absolute is thought of at rest, he called it Brahman. When it creates, sustains and dissolves the world, he called it Shakti, or Kali, or Mother.

teach.h: THE MOVING WORLD AS HER PLAY.
teach.b: If the moving world is Shakti, it isn't a distraction from the holy.
The cooking, the traffic, the growing, the grieving: in Shakta thought, that's the Goddess at work. Teachers in different schools put this differently.
Some describe the changing world as maya, a kind of appearance; Shakta teachers tend to speak of it as her play. This path holds both up and ranks neither.
For those who think the Shakta way, it's like the fire: you don't have to look past the heat to find the flame.

how: In Shakta traditions the Goddess is worshipped as the supreme reality, and some teachers in Ramakrishna's line still explain Brahman and Shakti with his images of fire and its burning, and the snake at rest and moving.

games.q: what does “shakti as a philosophy” mean?

a meditation on the breath at rest and moving
power to act, held by Shaktas to be the Goddess

games.q: someone asks you: is the still absolute one reality and the active Goddess another? what does Ramakrishna's picture say?
o: two realities, one above the other
one reality, like fire and its power to burn
only the still one is real
games.why: in the stories told by his followers, he says they're one: at rest he called it Brahman, acting he called it Shakti, or Mother.

practice: Look at a diya, a candle or a lamp if one is near, or bring a flame to mind, and notice that you can't pull the light apart from the warmth.

Then turn to your own body, the quiet awareness simply here and the breath moving through it, and rest in both at once without separating them. If you pray, hold the name Shakti, or Ma, gently; if you don't, stay with the flame.

wordCard.voice: Shakti as a philosophy. Power, energy, the ability to act, which Shakta traditions hold to be the Goddess herself, one with the absolute, the way fire is one with its burning. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit: shakti, power, energy, the ability to act; in Shakta traditions, the Goddess herself.

carryVoice: Your line: Shakti is the one reality in motion. Tomorrow, one verse about Shiva and Shakti. See you tomorrow.
